                                      PROJECT NO. 58481




RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT​      ​             ​       §             PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION​ ​               ​       §​     ​       ​     OF TEXAS
STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561​​             ​       §




      Comments of the Sierra Club on the Staff Discussion Draft (NEW 16 TAC §25.194)

                                     December 18th, 2025

Introduction

The Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club is the state chapter of the largest and oldest
conservation organization in the US. We have over 20,000 members in Texas, most of whom
reside within ERCOT. During the 89th legislative session, we supported SB 6, including provisions
requiring that certain large loads meet interconnection standards developed through
rulemaking at the PUCT (and associated protocols at ERCOT). As such, we appreciated the hard
work of PUCT staff and are largely supportive of the staff discussion draft released earlier this
year. Before turning to the specific provisions of the draft rule that we support - and where we
believe there is room for improvement - we wanted to provide an answer to the staff questions.

Answers to Staff Questions

1. Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load customer is
pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how should the commission
define those parameters?



                                                                                               1
 One of the issues which concerned policy makers and stakeholders during the 89th legislative
session was whether or not proposed large load interconnection requests were speculative in
nature, or were “real” and likely to actually occur. When no one can predict with certainty
whether a particular project will come to fruition in its beginning stages, policy makers and
many stakeholders are concerned when developers put forward nominal efforts for the same
project in several locations, sometimes in search of better tariffs, tax breaks or other factors.
While it is not illegal or unreasonable for such developers to look at multiple locations, Texas
and the grid could be impacted should cost be incurred and borne by other ratepayers for
projects that don’t come to bear, or forecasts could be widely optimistic about growth that then
doesn’t materialize. Therefore, Sierra Club believes it would be reasonable for the commission
to define parameters to determine whether a large load customer is pursuing a similar
interconnection request. Parameters could include the size, type of fuel, ownership, end-use
customer (if different than owner), use of backup generation and operational characteristics.
The Commission could also simply ask the customer to identify other interconnection requests
that represented the same load or project as it has done in the rule. We would agree that just
because an owner or developer has several projects that are similar in size and type in different
locations, does not by itself mean they are not separate “real” projects, so the Commission
must be careful to verify with the owner their intent.

2. Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific information​
related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows a large load customer to
anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the commission list what is and is not
competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not competitively sensitive information)? If so, what
information should and should not be considered competitively sensitive such that the
interconnecting utility and ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request, or a request
is unlikely to materialize?

There can be levels of competitively sensitive information and the Commission should identify
what is considered competitive and what is not. Recently, the Commission was involved in a
legal dispute over releasing information about bitcoin operations in Texas, and was required to
turn over information to new outlets that contained aggregated information on facilities
required to register with the commission. The Sierra Club is in favor of keeping most information
public and non-competitive to the extent it is basic such as location, size and fuel source (if
known) and presence of back-up power. Such basic information should also allow the
identification of duplicate requests. We understand that more specific information about
process equipment should remain competitive and not subject to public disclosure. We do not
see the need to spell out what is competitive and what is not.




                                                                                                 2
 3. Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the interconnecting electric
utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially disclosed in response to this rule
or only material changes to the information disclosed? If only material changes, how should
"material change" be defined?

We favor requiring large load customers to notify interconnecting electric utilities and ERCOT of
any change to information in response to this rule. Rather than trying to define material change,
requiring all large loads subject to the rule to notify their interconnecting utility and ERCOT of
any change will avoid issues down the road.

4. Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting electric utility to refund 20% of
a large load customer' s security after energization and ratably as the large load customer
meets the milestones identified in the customer' s schedule for phased energization of its
contracted load. Should the commission standardize the rate for refund for reaching milestones
identified in the customer's schedule for phased energization (e.g., 20% for each year of
operations until the full amount of security is refunded)? If so, how should the commission
standardize the refund?

We believe section (k) (1) and (k) (2) provides sufficient coverage by requiring an electric utility
to refund 20 percent of the security after the large load is energized and meets certain
milestones. The proposed rule already states that the remainder should be returned within five
years, but we believe this can be left up to the Commission, the utility and large load
agreement. Sierra Club would not object to such a standardization but also would not want to
dictate such terms, so long as ultimately customers are protected. In some cases, it might make
sense to return the security sooner, if it is clear the large load is energized, operating and has
met other requirements.

5. Are changes to the commission' s other substantive rules necessary to align with this
rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made to which rules?

As we have commented in several other related rules, we are of the opinion that Texas would be
best served by applying the requirements of SB 6 to all large loads of 25 MW or larger that are
connected at the transmission level as ERCOT has identified a need of this size. However, to the
extent that the Commission continues to only require that large loads of 75 MWs or larger be
subject to the provision of this rule, we still think there is a need for some consideration of
smaller loads to at least register with ERCOT and be considered in the forecasting rule. As we
discuss, we believe language could be added to this rule to allow smaller large loads to be
added to these requirements in the future.


                                                                                                      3
 Comment on proposed draft rule

The Sierra Club is largely in support of the proposed rule which would establish a standardized
process for interconnection agreements within ERCOT in an orderly, stepped process. Under the
proposed rule, the process indeed is well laid out and includes:

C) Disclosures and study fee upon request of interconnection request; d) Large load
interconnection study; e) Discretionary services agreement; f) submission of interconnection
study to ERCOT; g) notification of additional study (if needed) by ERCOT; h) Intermediate
Agreement, including financial security requirements; and then steps related to the withdrawal
of all or part of a project under (i) and finally, the actual terms for refund of financial security for
those large loads that are energizing. Subsection l establishes the process and ability for ERCOT
to establish operational standards for the large loads.

On the whole the Sierra Club is very supportive of the proposed rule. We appreciate the robust
financial security requirements, study process, potential for additional studies and ERCOT
operational control requirements as needed. While we understand that the proposed financial
security level of $50,000 per MW is high, the Commission is providing a variety of mechanisms
for large load customers to provide the financial security. If the Commission chooses,it could
also arrive at a tiered approach, such as $3 million for those facilities proposed between 25 and
100 MWs; $5 million for medium-sized large loads and $10 million for very large loads as
opposed to being so carefully tied to one number per MW, but we do not object to the
proposal.

Still, we would ask for consideration of three major changes to the proposal.

The Rule Establishes a 75 MW large load minimum but does not address loads below this
amount

The rule defines a large load as a “A customer requesting a new or expanded interconnection
where the customer' s total peak demand at a single site is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts
(MW).

The Public Utilities Regulatory Act ("PURA") § 37.0561 establishes a minimum threshold of 75
MWs at which a load would be considered "large" and subject to the requirements such as
interconnection standards. The Commission has authority, however, to expand its large load


                                                                                                      4
 interconnection requirements to include somewhat smaller loads. We urge the Commission to
make clear that the transmission interconnection rules apply to all new customers that are 25
MW or larger. At a recent PUCT open meeting, ERCOT staff indicated that there are some 14,000
MWs of large loads below 75 MWs that are seeking to interconnect with ERCOT at the
transmission level. This demonstrates the need to cast a wider net and include these entities in
the standardized interconnection process. Sierra Club is also concerned that once a rule that is
limited to those at 75 MWs and above is approved, then many developers may choose to
develop sites that are less than 75 MWs to avoid extra fees, more complex interconnection
processes or security investments. Indeed many large loads are coming in and interconnecting
at smaller levels - such as 50 MWs - and then planning to expand in the future as we see in
recent STEC transmission projects meant to incorporate large loads.

Making all large loads that are 25 MWs and above and interconnected at the transmission level
subject to these rules would be a good outcome for all consumers and the grid.

In short, while it is true that SB 6 requires the commission to create standards that apply to
large loads of 75 or more, it also allowed the Commission to set the threshold at a lower level if
it found it necessary for the good of the grid and to assure that there was good business
development but also to minimize the potential for stranded costs and to maintain system
reliability.

By putting this definition in the rule, the Commission is in essence preventing any requirements
for large loads under 75 MWs from having to meet the tough interconnections standards,
financial security and operational requirements. Sierra Club fears that large load customers will
choose to build smaller facilities that will not be subject to the same study, financial security
and other requirements, or even put several smaller facilities at one site that might equal 75
MWs but not at any single site. Therefore we recommend lowering the definition of large load
to a load of 25 MWs or more that is being interconnected at the transmission level.

If the Commission is not willing to apply the standards to loads below 75 MWs today, language
should be added that would allow for that potential in the future. Determining in 2025 or 2026
that only loads above 75 MWs must meet the standards in the rules seems short-sighted, and
we could consider language that would require the Commission to look at whether the
provisions of the rule should be applied to smaller loads within a certain time period.

The cost of the interconnection study and per MW fee should be staggered based on the size.




                                                                                                 5
 The Proposed rule suggests that those wishing to interconnect must either pay a $114,000 fee if
they are below 250 MWs or $314,000 if they are over 250 MWs. We would suggest instead
three tiers such as:

$114,000 for large loads between 25 MWs and 100 MWs;
$214,000 for large loads over 100 MWs and less than 300 MWs;
$314,000 for large loads between 300 and 500 MWs; and
$414,000 for large loads over 500 MWs.

This would more accurately reflect the variety of hypersized AI and datacenters being
contemplated.

Similarly the proposed rule suggests a flat $5,000 per MW fee for all large loads. We would
suggest that this fee could be staggered based on the size of the large load. That is, a larger load
- such as a load more than 250 MWs - might be subject to the $5,000 per MW fee, but smaller
loads could be charged a lower fee such as $3,000 per MW if they were under 100 MWs, or
$4,000 if they were between 100 and 250 MWs as an example.

Backup generating facilities should be better defined and required to provide additional
information to assure they are aware of air quality standards and permitting requirements for
backup generation

We agree that large load customers must provide information to the Commission (and ERCOT)
about their proposed use and the presence of backup generating facilities. However, we are first
concerned that the definition of backup generating facilities seems to limit it only to those
facilities providing at least 50% of the peak energy use of the facility which seems too high a
threshold for reporting. We understand that this definition – “Generation facilities that are not
capable of exporting energy to the ERCOT transmission system and that, in aggregate, can serve
at least 50% of on-site contracted peak demand” - is in part to align with statutory requirements
of when the PUCT can require a large load to use its backup generation, the definition is too
limiting and could mean that large loads with less than 50 percent of on-site contracted peak
demand are not being reported. We would suggest either removing the threshold or putting in
a lower threshold such as 20 percent. Language can be added in the rule to make it clear when
the PUCT can require the entity to use its backup generation.

Secondly, while we appreciate the detail in including the capacity, operating characteristics and
fuel use, there is no attention to any air quality permit requirements. Therefore, we would
suggest that the rule be expanded to require large loads to provide information about the EPA


                                                                                                    6
 Tier Ratings for any fossil-fuel power back up generators, and whether they must obtain any air
quality permits to operate the backup generators. Depending on the location of the facility,
assuring that the large load is in step with local, state and federal air quality regulations will be
key to assuring grid reliability and air quality, and making it more certain that that back up
generation will be available.

The Sierra Club appreciates the opportunity to make comments on the Staff’s proposed rule to
implement large load interconnection standards. We generally support the rule, including the
requirements for a study fee, financial security, and the potential to have to meet ERCOT
instructions for the use of the facility during an emergency. As discussed, we would prefer the
rule be applied to all large loads of 25 MWs or greater, we would require more information be
shared about backup generation, and believe the Commission should consider a wider range of
study fees and financial security.




                                                                                                        7
 Executive Summary, Sierra Club
Submitted by Cyrus Reed, Legislative and Conservation Director

The Sierra Club appreciates the opportunity to make comments on the Staff’s proposed rule to
implement large load interconnection standards. We generally support the rule, including the
requirements for a study fee, financial security, and the potential to have to meet ERCOT
instructions for the use of the facility during an emergency. As discussed, we would prefer the
rule be applied to all large loads of 25 MWs or greater, we would require more information be
shared about backup generation, and believe the Commission should consider a wider range of
study fees and financial security.

First, we are concerned by the decision to only apply the rule to large loads of 75 MWs or larger
(at a single interconnection point), and instead would apply at least some of the requirements
to loads that are 25 MWs or greater that are interconnected at the transmission level. If the
Commission wants to narrowly apply the rule only to those at 75 MWs or greater currently to
meet the specific requirements of SB 6, we would ask that the commission consider some
language about applying the rule to smaller large loads in the future.

While we support the required study fee and financial security amounts found in the proposed
rule, we would suggest a range of fees based on size. In other words, the proposed rule only
provides two potential study fees - $114,000 or $314,000 - but we would suggest a wider range
based on MW size between $114,000 to $414,000 depending on size. In terms of financial
security, while we are supportive of the $5,000 per MW proposal, another option would be to
charge large loads based on a flat fee per range of MWs, with a slightly lower amount per MW
for smaller loads. In our proposal the amount per MW could vary between $3,000 and $5,000
per MW. .

Finally, we are concerned that the definition of backup generation is too limiting, and might
limit reporting of a large load’s backup generation. We would remove the 50% threshold or
lower it. We would also require the large load to provide specific information about engine
levels, tiers and air pollution permit or regulation requirements. The PUCT and the public has a
right to know if the backup generation being developed will be able to operate under modern
air quality standards and regulations to assure it is effective.




                                                                                                   8
 Respectfully submitted,

Dr. Cyrus Reed, PhD
Conservation Director
Lone Star Chapter, Sierra Club
6406 North I-35, Suite 1806
Austin, Texas 78752
Tel: 512-888-9411
Email: Cyrus.reed@sierraclub.org

While we support the required study fee and financial security amounts found in the proposed
rule, we would suggest a range of fees based on size. In other words, the proposed rule only
provides two potential study fees - $114,000 or $314,000 - but we would suggest a wider range
based on MW size between $114,000 to $414,000 depending on size. In terms of financial
security, while we are supportive of the $5,000 per MW proposal, another option would be to
charge large loads based on a flat fee per range of MWs, with a slightly lower amount per MW
for smaller loads. In our proposal the amount per MW could vary between $3,000 and $5,000
per MW .


Finally, we are concerned that the definition of backup generation is too limiting, and might
limit reporting of a large load's backup generation. We would remove the 50% threshold or
lower it. We would also require the large load to provide specific information about engine
levels, tiers and air pollution permit or regulation requirements. The PUCT and the public has a
right to know if the backup generation being developed will be able to operate under modern
air quality standards and regulations to assure it is effective.
